summary: Describes the syntax and procedures for computing and verifying digital signatures in version 1.0 of the Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP). Signatures let parties in a trade check who sent a message and that it was not altered. It is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: A signature on a paper check shows who wrote it. This explains how to put a digital signature on online shopping messages so others can check who sent them.

subtitle: Digital signatures for secure online commerce messages in IOTP.

tldr.problem: Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) messages are XML documents exchanged during online commerce. Parties need to authenticate messages (prove who sent them) and detect tampering, but IOTP Version 1.0 does not have general XML digital signature support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Signature XML element containing a Manifest (authenticated attributes including digests of the data being signed, originator info, and algorithm references) and a Value (the encrypted signature itself). Signatures are computed by canonicalizing and digesting the Manifest, then encrypting the digest using the signer's private key or a shared secret.
tldr.outcome: IOTP messages can be signed to provide authentication and integrity. The design is lightweight, supports multiple signature algorithms, and allows signatures to be forwarded to other recipients with different algorithms.

today: RFC 2802 is informational and describes IOTP Version 1.0 signatures. While IOTP itself did not see widespread adoption, the digital signature concepts and XML structure principles documented here influenced later XML digital signature standards. The W3C eventually published XML-Signature (XML-DSig), which became the standard for signing XML documents, superseding this approach for general use. However, this RFC remains a historical reference for IOTP implementations and demonstrates the design challenges of adding signatures to XML-based protocols.

sections.title: IOTP and the Need for Signatures
sections.content:
The Internet Open Trading Protocol (IOTP) provides a framework for online commerce independent of any particular payment system, using XML as its message format. Although IOTP assumes the underlying payment system provides security, the protocol itself requires authentication and integrity protection for many message exchanges: proving who created a transaction, detecting if an order was altered in transit, or ensuring a payment token was not modified.

While general XML digital signature standards were under development in 1999, they were unlikely to be ready in time for IOTP Version 1.0. This RFC defines a practical signature syntax and procedures specifically for IOTP, with the expectation that future versions would adopt the eventual standard.

The design objectives include ease of integration with IOTP, lightweight signatures with minimal redundancy, support for multiple signature algorithms, and the ability to forward signed message portions to other parties with different signature algorithms than the original recipient.
sections.eli5: Shopping online, you send a message describing what you want to buy. You need to prove it was you who sent it and that nobody changed the order. This explains how to add a special mark to the message to prove that.

sections.title: How Digital Signatures Work in IOTP
sections.content:
The Signature element consists of two sub-elements. The Manifest contains authenticated attributes: references to the data being signed (via Digest elements), information about the originator and recipient, algorithm specifications, and optional custom attributes.

The Digest element contains a locator (reference) to a resource and a digest value computed from that resource using a specified digest algorithm. The locator can reference internal IOTP message elements by ID or external resources by URL. Digests allow the signature to cover multiple resources without including them inline in the signature.

The OriginatorInfo element is mandatory and provides identification and keying material: either a reference to a digital certificate or a unique identifier known to the recipient. The RecipientInfo element is optional and specifies which recipient(s) the signature is intended for, allowing one IOTP message to contain multiple signatures for different parties.

The Value element contains the digital signature itself—the result of digesting the canonicalized Manifest and encrypting it with the signer's private key (for public-key signatures) or a shared secret (for message authentication codes).
sections.eli5: A signature has two parts. First, a list of things being signed (like the order details and who the buyer is). Second, a secret encrypted code that proves the buyer signed it.

sections.title: The Three-Step Signing Process
sections.content:
Creating a signature involves three steps. Canonicalization converts the XML Manifest to a standard form, removing inconsistencies in whitespace and formatting that XML parsers may introduce. This ensures that the same logical Manifest always produces the same byte sequence.

Digest computation applies a digest algorithm (such as SHA-1) to the canonicalized Manifest to produce a fingerprint. Any change in the Manifest produces a very different digest.

Signature computation encrypts the digest using a signature algorithm (DSA, RSA, HMAC, or ECDSA) with the signer's private key or a shared secret. This final encrypted value is stored in the Signature's Value element.

To verify a signature, the recipient canonicalizes and digests the received Manifest, then decrypts the signature value using the signer's public key (or the shared secret). If the decrypted value matches the computed digest, the signature is valid—proving the Manifest came from the claimed signer and was not altered.
sections.eli5: First, format the message nicely. Second, compute a fingerprint of it. Third, encrypt that fingerprint with a secret key. Checking it means redoing those steps and seeing if the fingerprint matches.

sections.title: Supported Algorithms
sections.content:
IOTP 1.0 requires implementation of four algorithms: DSA (a public-key signature algorithm), DOM-HASH (a canonical XML digest that understands DOM structure), SHA-1 (a standard 160-bit digest), and HMAC (a message authentication code using a shared secret). Implementation of RSA is recommended but not mandatory.

DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm) is NIST's public-key signature standard. It requires a digest algorithm as a parameter, typically DOM-HASH. It produces a pair of integers (r,s) encoded as octet streams.

SHA-1 is a surface-string digest algorithm that hashes any input to a 160-bit fingerprint. Changes in whitespace or formatting affect the digest.

DOM-HASH is a canonical digest algorithm that understands XML's Document Object Model (DOM) tree structure, computing hashes recursively from leaf to root. It is better suited to small documents and requires SHA-1 as a sub-parameter.

HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) computes an authentication code using a shared secret key and a hash function (typically SHA-1). It provides authentication without public-key infrastructure, useful when parties have a prior relationship. It requires three parameters: a canonical digest algorithm, a hash function, and an optional output length for truncation.

RSA is the widely-used public-key encryption algorithm, applying PKCS#1 padding and encrypting the digest with the signer's private key.

ECDSA (Elliptic Curve DSA) provides the same security as DSA using smaller keys through elliptic curve mathematics.
sections.eli5: Several ways to create and verify signatures: DSA and RSA and ECDSA use public-key cryptography (everyone has your public key), while HMAC uses a shared secret. SHA-1 and DOM-HASH are ways to compute the fingerprint.

sections.title: XML Signature Syntax
sections.content:
The top-level element is IotpSignatures, containing one or more Signature elements and optional Certificate elements. Each Signature element contains exactly one Manifest and one or more Value elements (allowing multiple algorithms in one signature).

The Manifest contains: Algorithm elements specifying digest and signature algorithms; Digest elements each with a locator and value for resources being authenticated; optional Attribute elements for custom properties; mandatory OriginatorInfo; and one or more RecipientInfo elements specifying which recipient(s) each signature is intended for and which algorithm to use for verification.

The Algorithm element has a required ID attribute (for cross-referencing), a type (digest or signature), and a name expressed as a Uniform Resource Name (URN). It may contain Parameter elements specifying sub-algorithms or other settings. For example, a DSA algorithm parameter specifies which digest algorithm to use, and an HMAC parameter specifies the hash function and optional output truncation length.

The Certificate element provides X.509 version 3 certificates, either inline as a base-64-encoded value or by reference (locator). It requires an IssuerAndSerialNumber for unambiguous identification.

All text content (digests, signature values, certificates) is base-64 encoded unless explicitly marked otherwise.
sections.eli5: The signature goes in a Manifest block that says which algorithm to use, what resources are signed, and who the sender and recipients are. The actual signature value goes in a Value block. Certificates can be included if needed.
